title: Nimitz-class aircraft carrier
description: US Navy nuclear-powered aircraft carrier class
wiki_lead:
The Nimitz class is a class of ten nuclear-powered aircraft carriers in service with the United States Navy. The lead ship of the class is named after World War II United States Pacific Fleet commander Fleet Admiral Chester W. Nimitz, who was the last living U.S. Navy officer to hold the rank. With an overall length of 1,092 ft (333 m) and a full-load displacement of over 100,000 long tons (100,000 t), the Nimitz-class ships were the largest warships built and in service until USS Gerald R. Ford entered the fleet in 2017.
Instead of the gas turbines or diesel–electric systems used for propulsion on many modern warships, the carriers use two A4W nuclear pressurized water reactors. The reactors produce steam to drive steam turbines which drive four propeller shafts and can produce a maximum speed of over 30 knots (56 km/h; 35 mph) and a maximum power of around 260,000 shaft horsepower (190 MW). As a result of nuclear power, the ships are capable of operating for over 20 years without refueling and are predicted to have a service life of over 50 years. They are categorized as nuclear-powered aircraft carriers and are numbered with consecutive hull numbers from CVN-68 to CVN-77.
All ten carriers were constructed by Newport News Shipbuilding Company in Virginia. USS Nimitz, the lead ship of the class, was commissioned on 3 May 1975, and USS George H. W. Bush, the tenth and last of the class, was commissioned on 10 January 2009. Since the 1970s, Nimitz-class carriers have participated in many conflicts and operations across the world, including Operation Eagle Claw in Iran, the Gulf War, and more recently in Iraq and Afghanistan.
The angled flight decks of the carriers use a CATOBAR arrangement to operate aircraft, with steam catapults and arrestor wires for launch and recovery. As well as speeding up flight deck operations, this allows for a much wider variety of aircraft than with the STOVL arrangement used on smaller carriers. An embarked carrier air wing comprising around 64 aircraft is normally deployed on board. The air wings' strike fighters are primarily F/A-18E and F/A-18F Super Hornets. In addition to their aircraft, the vessels carry short-range defensive weaponry for anti-aircraft warfare and missile defense.
The unit cost was about US$8.5 billion in FY 2012 dollars, equal to US$11.8 billion in 2025.

grok_lead: The Nimitz -class aircraft carrier comprises a series of ten nuclear-powered supercarriers commissioned into service with the United States Navy from 1975 to 2009, forming the backbone of American naval aviation capabilities during the late Cold War and post-Cold War eras. The U.S. Navy's current supercarrier classes are the Nimitz-class (10 ships in service) and the Gerald R. Ford-class (lead ship in service, others under construction or testing as of 2026), with older classes like Kitty Hawk-class and Enterprise retired. Named in honor of Fleet Admiral Chester W. Nimitz, who commanded the Pacific Fleet during World War II, the lead ship USS Nimitz (CVN-68) was laid down in 1968 and commissioned on May 3, 1975, with subsequent vessels constructed at Newport News Shipbuilding in Virginia. These vessels displace approximately 100,000 long tons at full load, measure 1,092 feet (333 meters) in overall length, and feature a flight deck spanning 4.5 acres, enabling the embarkation of a carrier air wing typically consisting of 60 to 90 fixed-wing and rotary-wing aircraft for strike, reconnaissance, and support missions. Powered by two A4W pressurized water reactors producing over 260,000 shaft horsepower, the Nimitz -class carriers achieve speeds in excess of 30 knots and possess an operational range limited only by provisions and munitions, with reactors designed for a 20- to 25-year service life before mid-life refueling during complex overhauls. Each carrier supports a crew of over 5,000 sailors and aviators, including ship operations personnel and the air wing, underscoring their role as self-contained floating airbases capable of projecting decisive air power thousands of miles from U.S. shores without reliance on foreign bases. The class's defining characteristics include advanced catapults for rapid aircraft launches, angled flight decks for simultaneous operations, and integrated defensive systems such as Sea Sparrow missiles and Phalanx close-in weapons, which have enabled sustained deployments in high-threat environments and contributed to U.S. naval supremacy through superior endurance and firepower. Despite their immense capabilities, the vessels have faced challenges including high construction and maintenance costs exceeding billions per ship and vulnerabilities exposed in exercises to modern anti-ship threats, prompting the transition to the follow-on Gerald R. Ford-class, which measures 1,106 ft (337 m) overall, with a beam of 256 ft (78 m) on the flight deck and 134 ft (41 m) at the waterline, and a draft of 39 ft (12 m), featuring enhanced automation and stealth features.
